_comment: QUI-992 Flux v8 app spec for the Quip testnet Blockscout explorer.
NOT DEPLOYED. Starting point for the dashboard wizard only — the canonical
spec is always the dashboard EXPORT, never a file in this repo. Enterprise
apps return `compose: []` from the public API, so keep the export locally.
Note the comments live HERE and not inside the compose entries: the compose
objects are kept to exactly the fields Flux validates, so this file can be
pasted or imported without an unknown-key rejection.
── RESOURCE SHAPE IS MEASURED, NOT GUESSED ─────────────────────────────
From the QUI-992 rehearsal against the live endpoint (2026-08-11, ~107k
block backfill sustained at 22.4 blocks/s):
bsapi   465 MiB RSS, 0.55-0.82 core during catchup (the heaviest phase)
bsdb    359 MiB RSS, 2-6% of a core
bsui    186 MiB RSS, idle
bsproxy  10 MiB RSS, idle
Every allocation is ~4x its measured peak, except bsproxy which sits at
nginx's practical floor. Upstream Blockscout's published 16-core / 128 GB
sizing is for Ethereum mainnet and does not describe this chain.
TOTALS: 2.75 cpu / 4500 MB / 103 GB. The cpu total is deliberately under 3:
Flux applies a 0.8x multiplier when instances<4 AND cpu<3 AND ram<6000 AND
hdd<150, so crossing 3.0 cpu costs roughly a third more for headroom the
measurements say we do not need. A cpu or ram change later needs a NEW
subscription but does NOT destroy the volume — only an hdd change does — so
this is a cheap decision to revise upward if the explorer feels slow.
Verify the real figure in the dashboard calculator before subscribing; it
is authoritative and this arithmetic is not.
Measured growth is 1693 bytes/block = 8.2 GiB/year at the current
(near-empty) block profile, so 100 GB is over a decade of runway. It is
oversized on purpose: blocks only get heavier as EVM usage arrives, and
changing hdd is a HARD redeploy that DESTROYS the volume on every instance.
At $0.02/GB it is the cheapest insurance in this spec.
Adding or removing a COMPONENT later is also a hard redeploy that wipes all
volumes. That is tolerable and is deliberately not designed around:
Blockscout's Postgres is 100% derived state, so the recovery is a
re-backfill from FIRST_BLOCK (~80 min at the rehearsed rate). Nothing in it
is authoritative and it is deliberately not backed up.
instances is 1 (legal: minimumInstancesV8 is 1). No redundancy — a host
relocation means fresh volumes and a full re-backfill. Acceptable for a
read-only explorer whose data is reconstructible.
bsdb  repotag is the multi-arch manifest LIST digest; Docker resolves the
amd64 child sha256:af194ccf3e2d7fe367012c7b88ce8b816c5c889b18a5b3167
99a1f0d7eac746a. Pinned to the exact image the rehearsal ran against —
a floating tag is how a fleet drifts silently.
PGDATA points at a SUBDIRECTORY of the mount. A fresh Flux volume is
an ext4 filesystem whose root is not empty (lost+found) and is
root-owned; initdb refuses a non-empty PGDATA. Creating it one level
down sidesteps both without relying on the entrypoint's chown.
`commands` is EMPTY on purpose. An earlier revision raised
max_connections to 200 here, because Blockscout's default pools open
~100 connections and hold them idle — exhausting Postgres's default
budget and producing 'sorry, too many clients already' for everything
else. That treated the symptom. The pools are capped in the image
instead (POOL_SIZE=20 / POOL_SIZE_API=10), which measured 100 -> 31
connections and Postgres RSS 469 -> ~150 MiB with no change in
indexing rate. 31 sits comfortably inside the default 100, so the
server needs no override at all.
It publishes NOTHING. Flux's Docker DNAT makes external clients appear
to come from 172.x, so 'it came from private space' is not an
authorization check on this network.
bsapi Carries only the two real secrets. Everything else is baked via
--build-arg BAKE_PROD_ENV=1, because Flux hard-caps each component at
20 env vars and Blockscout needs far more. The DB host is Flux's
flux<component>_<appname> DNS name — never the 172.23.x address, which
is per-host and changes on relocation.
bsui  No secrets at all: every NEXT_PUBLIC_* is shipped to the browser by
definition, so all of it is baked and this component's env is empty.
bsproxy 20050 is the ONLY published port. It is outside Flux's banned ranges
and is NOT an enterprise port (0-1023, 8080, 8081, 8443, 6667), each of
which adds a surcharge before the price divisor. It serves PLAIN HTTP:
FDM terminates TLS and re-originates cleartext, so in-container TLS
would make the app unreachable through FDM.
`domains` is left [""] deliberately — the custom domain is applied in
the dashboard AFTER the CNAME resolves, per the proven CNAME-first
ordering. domains is a parallel array to ports and Flux enforces equal
length, so it must stay length 1.
Every component declares a containerData (Flux requires min length 2);
/tmp is the documented placeholder for the stateless ones.
⚠ ENTERPRISE (ENCRYPTED) IS PROBABLY REQUIRED — UNRESOLVED.
`enterprise` is "" below, i.e. a plain public app. That is very likely
WRONG for this spec. A non-enterprise app's `compose` is readable from
Flux's public API, and `environmentParameters` is part of compose — which
would publish SECRET_KEY_BASE and the Postgres password to anyone who asks
the network for the app spec. Enterprise apps return `compose: []` from
that API instead, which is exactly why the bootnodes keep their secrets in
the encrypted `secrets` field.
This is required for the app's OWN two secrets and would be even if the
registry were private. Making the GitLab project public removed the
registry token from the spec; it did not remove the reason for encryption.
Impact if we ignore it: the Postgres password guards a component that
publishes no port, so it is only reachable from inside the app's own
network — low value, but not nothing on a shared host. SECRET_KEY_BASE
signs cookies for an explorer with no accounts — also low, also not
something to publish deliberately.
Cost of fixing: enterprise adds 4.00 to the pre-divisor total, so roughly
$4.00/month instead of $3.20. The 0.8x discount still applies (it keys on
instances/cpu/ram/hdd, not on the enterprise flag).
Decide this BEFORE subscribing: switching later means a new subscription.
0. The GitLab project quip.network/explorer.quip.network must EXIST. The
container registry lives under the project, so nothing can be pushed
until it does, and every step below depends on that push.
1. Build and push the three images: PUSH=1 scripts/build-images.sh
Then replace the three <REPLACE-*> repotags. ⚠ The value must be
repo:TAG@sha256:DIGEST — a BARE digest is rejected. FluxOS's
ImageVerifier.imagePattern (imageVerifier.js:14) parses only
[HOST/][NAMESPACE/]REPOSITORY[:TAG] and has no @sha256: branch, so a bare
`repo@sha256:...` parses as namespace=repo, repository='', tag=undefined
and the dashboard rejects it with "Authentication failed: ... not
available or doesn't exist" — which reads like a credentials problem and
is not one. With the tag present the regex stops at the '@' and ignores
the digest tail, while Docker still honours the digest on pull.
scripts/validate-spec.py now enforces this. Note the dashboard reports
only the FIRST bad component, so fix all four at once.
2. Create the DNSimple CNAME explorer.testnet.quip.network ->
quipexplorer.app.runonflux.io and confirm it resolves to fdm-lb-*
BEFORE applying the Custom Domain. Applying first pushes FDM's ACME
into backoff.
3. Nothing to mint: the GitLab project is PUBLIC, so its registry is
anonymously pullable and `repoauth` stays EMPTY on every component.
Do NOT put a placeholder there — Flux sends it verbatim and the
registry answers 401 rather than falling back to anonymous.
4. Generate a fresh SECRET_KEY_BASE (openssl rand -hex 64). Do NOT reuse
the rehearsal value or the dev literal from !65.
No dnsimple-certifier, no flux-dns-controller registry entry and no Tarsnap
cert seeding are involved. FDM owns issuance and renewal. That is the whole
reason this deployment satisfies 'cert renewal not manual' with no local
renewal loop to maintain.
name: quipexplorer
description: Quip testnet Blockscout EVM explorer (indexes the QUI-966 eth-rpc endpoint).

compose.name: bsdb
compose.description: Postgres 17 for Blockscout. Derived state only — not backed up.

compose.name: bsapi
compose.description: Blockscout backend: indexer + API. All non-secret config baked into the image.

compose.name: bsui
compose.description: Blockscout Next.js frontend. No secrets; all NEXT_PUBLIC_* config is baked.

compose.name: bsproxy
compose.description: nginx single-origin front: frontend at /, backend at /api, /socket, /sitemap.xml.
